newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: ABB CEO says 1996 result excellent.
newsitem.headline: ABB CEO says 1996 result excellent.

text.p: Goran Lindahl, the new president and chief executive of ABB Asea Brown Boveri AG, said a drop in the company's share price was probably due to the company's 1997 forecast rather than disappointment over 1996 results, which he characterised as excellent.

Lindahl told reporters after the company's annual news conference that he had no specific view of the share price of ABB's two quoted parent companies, but it was important that ABB gave credible forecasts and ABB's operations had improved in 1996 from 1995.
"If we can keep at least the same (profit) level for 1997 as in 1996, then we come out of the recession, the downturn in the economy, much better when compared with the last," Lindahl said.

ABB reported a 6.2 percent decline in its 1996 group net profit from 1995's profit which was inflated by a one-off gain of $250 million in connection with a transportation venture with Germany's Daimler-Benz AG.
Excluding the one-off gain, ABB's net profit rose 15.8 percent to $1.233 billion from an adjusted $1.065 billion.
Lindahl said ABB had clearly warned markets about the slowdown in 1996 and 1997 and its 1996 results should be compared with the adjusted 1995 results.
"The operations were definitely better in 1996 than in 1995," Lindahl said.
ABB also forecast that its 1997 net profit would at least reach the 1996 level.
Asked about the forecast, Lindahl said it meant that he had established a floor for 1997 profits and "you don't start drilling through the floor."
The stock market reacted with disappointment to ABB's results and shares of its Swiss parent, ABB AG, fell by 4.4 percent on the Swiss Exchange to 1,730 francs in late afternoon trade.

Although Lindahl declined to elaborate on the 1997 forecast or business so far this year, he said he was convinced market conditions would start to improve during 1997 and by 2000 ABB would be at the peak of its next business cycle.
As a capital goods company, ABB is late in the economic cycles and earnings in 1996 and 1997 will be depressed by the slowdown in Europe.
Lindahl, who took over as chief executive from Percy Barnevik on January 1, said he was optimistic about ABB's direction as it continued to expand in emerging markets.
The shift of production into low-cost countries coupled with increasing service and revamping business should boost margins.
"The mix will create higher margins overall in our business so that should be reassuring to anyone interested in ABB," Lindahl said.
Asked whether ABB remained committed to its 50 percent stake in the Adtranz venture with Daimler, Lindahl said ABB was committed to the transportation business for the long term and believed in it.

Despite a 39 percent decline in 1996 operating earnings at ABB's Power Generation segment, Lindahl said the results were still extremely good under present circumstances and a margin of almost six percent was good compared with other competitors.
Lindahl said the power generation business had never been in a critical state, but the price war had taken a bite out of profits.

However, last year's investments in technology and a restructuring of the power business, including the sourcing from low cost suppliers in such countries as Poland and India, would start to pay back in higher business volumes, more cost efficiency and lower costs, Lindahl said.
